claims.text: The initial CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles are a uniformly crystallized homogeneous solid solution.
Stability of CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles across 473–1923 K is governed by competition between kinetically limited diffusion and thermally activated segregation.
Slow atomic diffusion relative to the thermal ramp rate maintains structural and chemical uniformity.
Maintaining structural and chemical uniformity preserves catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
Overcoming kinetic barriers at elevated temperature accelerates atomic diffusion.
Substantial atomic diffusion induces local elemental segregation and compositional heterogeneity.
Elemental segregation causes formation of new phases and phase instability.
Segregation and phase instability degrade catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
The relevant structural mediator is the degree of elemental segregation and short-range ordering.
Five-element alloy nanoparticles can retain a random elemental distribution with only short-range compositional fluctuations under some modeled conditions.
An inert atmosphere with an optimal temperature ramp rate promotes slow diffusion.
Oxidizing or reducing atmospheres lower diffusion barriers and make diffusion significant.
Slow-diffusion conditions will retain a uniform solid solution.
Conditions producing significant diffusion will yield measurable local compositional variations.
Local compositional variations will correspond to declines in catalytic activity and thermoelectric figure of merit.
The initial nanoparticles have stable catalytic and thermoelectric properties before thermal cycling.
The prediction applies when atmospheric composition and temperature ramp rate are carefully controlled.
Impurities or extreme heating rates can artificially enhance atomic mobility.
The critical diffusion threshold for segregation and the quantitative segregation–performance relationship are unknown.
Comparable segregation or performance degradation in the nominally slow- and accelerated-diffusion groups would falsify the proposed kinetic-stabilization hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis implies that diffusion remaining slow relative to a faster thermal ramp favors retention of homogeneity, whereas the experimental design labels higher ramp rates as diffusion-accelerating and the boundary statement says extreme heating rates enhance atomic mobility.
